prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: [val] Code · CLI flags (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Flag" · longest unbreakable unit 106px · widest one-line content 204px
  col 2: header "Type" · longest unbreakable unit 55px · widest one-line content 55px
  col 3: header "Default" · longest unbreakable unit 114px · widest one-line content 114px
  col 4: header "Description" · longest unbreakable unit 89px · widest one-line content 477px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 360px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). At 360px some words cannot fit unsplit. Horizontal scrolling is ALLOWED: the table may be wider than 360px (column widths summing to more than 359px) (the reader scrolls), or you may fit within 359px and accept the consequences. Fitting and scrolling layouts are judged as two separate classes; propose good layouts of BOTH kinds.
Rendering convention: a full render shows the WHOLE table; anything right of the dashed box is not clipped — it is reached by scrolling. Where a layout scrolls, an extra "viewport view" image shows only what is visible at first sight.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Help readers choose and use CLI flags by connecting each flag to its type, default value, and behavior.","tasks":["Look up a known flag and check its default or accepted type.","Compare flags and defaults across rows.","Read descriptions to understand what each option does."],"relations":["Each row describes one flag or set of aliases; its type, default, and description belong together.","The flag is the primary lookup key, while the description explains its effect."],"roles":["Column headers label four distinct fields; the body rows are peer entries.","The flag column anchors lookup, the type and default columns provide compact reference values, and the description column carries explanatory prose."],"keep_whole":["Flag names and aliases where possible, especially --experimental-vm-modules and --inspect-brk=[host]:port.","Type names, numeric defaults, false, and the address 127.0.0.1:9229."],"may_wrap":["Description prose at word boundaries.","Multiple flag aliases between aliases when space requires it."],"same_scale":["Body rows share the same reference role, although descriptions may naturally make some rows taller.","Type and default are both short reference fields, but the address default needs more width than any type."],"h_vs_v":"At phone width the minimum widths needed to keep the longest units whole exceed the viewport. A fitting table forces breaks inside identifiers and values and makes rows taller; scrolling preserves those units and gives descriptions more natural lines, at the cost of hiding some columns initially."}

Image 1 is the one-line content overview. Then real browser renders of: d1r0A, d1r0B (full view, then viewport view), d1r0C (full view, then viewport view).
Measured facts:
d1r0A: column widths [105, 59, 85, 110] px · table 360×578 px · row heights [36, 153, 153, 106, 129] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 6 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 7 · fits the 360 px viewport (no scrolling)
d1r0B: column widths [225, 76, 135, 190] px · table 627×345 px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 60, 83] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 267 px (horizontal scrolling)
d1r0C: column widths [145, 76, 135, 340] px · table 697×252 px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 337 px (horizontal scrolling)

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). This is your first look at real renders: propose at least one improved or alternative design (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or test an important idea you have not tried). "done" is not allowed yet. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
